answers.text: Signing authority was formally two officers, the treasurer and the president, but in practice the advisor countersigned anything over five hundred dollars because the bank wanted a staff signature on the larger transfers, and nobody ever went back and wrote that practice into the bylaws.

Dues are the thing everyone gets wrong. The written figure is thirty-five, which is what the constitution says, but the membership voted to raise it to forty at the October meeting and the treasurer simply started collecting forty. The document was never amended, so both numbers are live in our records.

The bank change happened in January and it caused most of this confusion. We moved accounts, the old statements stop mid-year, and the new ones start with a different account number, so anyone reading the two side by side would think there were two accounts running at once. There was only ever one.

Quorum is genuinely ambiguous in our documents. One section says a third of active members and a later amendment says half of voting members, and those were written four years apart by different secretaries. In practice we counted a third, and no vote was ever challenged on that basis.

Reimbursement went through me because I kept the folder, but the actual approval was the advisor's. I would collect the receipt, put it in the shared drive, and the advisor would sign off before anything moved. That two-step is why the minutes sometimes name the secretary and sometimes name the advisor for the same payment.

I want to be careful here because I only saw the second half of that year. What I can tell you is that the vendor contract was not renewed, the last invoice I processed was in March, and anything after that in the records is either a duplicate entry or a payment I did not handle myself.

The officer terms overlap on paper and that is not an error. Our handover runs from the April election to the end of May, so the outgoing and incoming officers are both listed as holding the role for about six weeks. Someone reading the roster without knowing that would call it a contradiction.

Honestly, the spreadsheet is the least reliable document we have. It has no headers, three people edited it, and at least one column is a running balance that someone re-sorted alphabetically at some point. I would trust the bank export and the minutes over anything in that file.

The petty cash figure changed midyear. It started at fifty because that is what the previous treasurer left in the tin, and after the fall fundraiser we raised the float to a hundred so the events team could buy supplies without waiting on a transfer. Both numbers appear in the records and both were true, at different times.

That policy exists but nobody followed it. The constitution requires two weeks notice for a budget vote, and in practice we gave a few days because the room booking deadline moved. If you are asking what the rule says versus what we actually did, those are two different answers and I would rather give you both.

The advisor kept the second key to the storage room and the treasurer kept the first, and that arrangement was never written down anywhere I could find. I only learned it because I needed the room in September and had to ask three people before someone told me where the key lived.

The October minutes and the November minutes disagree because the November set was written from memory two weeks late. I would treat the October set as the accurate one; it was taken live in the meeting and its attendance list matches the sign-in sheet exactly.

There were two grant applications that year and people conflate them. The first was submitted in the fall and rejected, the second went in the following spring under a different program and was funded. The records refer to both as the grant, which is why the amounts do not line up.

I would not describe that as a disagreement so much as a gap. The constitution says the treasurer maintains the account. It does not say who has read access, who reconciles it, or what happens when the treasurer is unreachable in August, and every one of those questions came up while I held the role.

The transition folder is real but it is incomplete. It has the bank letter, the tax form, and last year's budget, and it does not have the vendor contacts, the room booking login, or the advisor's preferred process for reimbursements. Those three things are what I spent my first month learning.

Both documents are describing the same decision from different sides. The minutes record that the motion passed, and the budget sheet records the amount that was actually spent, which was lower because the event ran under budget. Neither one is wrong; they are answering different questions.

The short answer is that we changed the process halfway through and only half the paperwork caught up. Before December, requests went to the treasurer directly. After December, they went through a form the advisor set up, and the older records never got migrated into it.

I can tell you what I saw, but I want to flag that I was not in the room for the vote itself. What I have is the minutes I typed from someone else's notes, and I would rank that below the sign-in sheet and well below the bank record if you are trying to establish what actually happened.
